place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 外门 · 告示栏
place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the notice board

setup.zh: 开山门那一夜：女弟子的大通铺上，一个红鼻头的姑娘在小本子上记账；男弟子的大通铺上，马小宝跟两个老弟子嘀咕到半夜。告示栏上，墨迹未干。
setup.en: The night the gate opened: on the girls' long bunk, a red-nosed girl keeps accounts in her little notebook; on the boys', Ma Xiaobao whispers with two old disciples past midnight. On the notice board, the ink is not yet dry.

recap.zh: 外门第一夜：马小宝成了「马师兄」，告示栏上贴出公中告示——每人先交一块。
recap.en: The first night in the outer court: Ma Xiaobao became "Senior Brother Ma", and the common-fund notice went up — one stone each, paid first.

zh: 外门的告示栏，墨迹未干。
en: The outer court's notice board, ink still wet.

story.zh:
话分两头。外门女弟子的大通铺，在另一个院子里。那一夜，最靠墙的一张铺上，有一盏豆大的油灯还亮着。灯底下趴着一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘，红鼻头，拿一截新削的炭条，在一个巴掌大的小本子上，一笔一画地写。她写的是：

九月初九。重阳。

石阶。三百级。冲上去的，没坐。脚底磨了两个泡，记：左一，右一。

他在后头，走的，不跑。三步一口气，像他爹。马小宝的滑竿堵他，他从底下钻过去了。

洛书。我摆好的时候，他还在发呆。后来他摆对了，比我慢半炷香。老执事问他为什么，他说是算的。记：他有口诀，还算。我没口诀，只算。

林子。那东西九个头。我是闭着眼睛走过去摸的树皮，没看它。他看了，还扔了石头。他往右滚那一下，我没看懂，像是有人跟他说了什么。记：问。不问。先记着。

马家的人往林子里扔了一颗石子。我看见了。扫地的老头也看见了。记。

测灵石。我，三种，他们说中上。他，五种，他们笑。我没笑。马小宝笑了三声，记：三声。

名额满了，他举着牌子说了一句话，殿里就不笑了。记：他敢。

他没认出我。

娘说：去。娘说：别跟他一路走。一个人去会死，两个人一起去，死一双，不划算。娘说完就哭了。爹送我走的小路，比他们早走一天，住在庙廊底下。

记：娘，欠我一个不哭。

五两。弟弟。

禾种三十粒，缝在袄里。

爹背我走了一段。过了老槐树，爹说：「过了这棵树，就不是咱村了。」他把我放下来，让我自己走。我回头看了一眼。那棵树，我在树底下站了十一年，今天才知道，从外头看，它这么小。

记：沈小满，欠我鸡蛋三个半。利息，另算。

写到这里，油灯的芯子「噼」地爆了一下。那姑娘抬起头来，看了看窗外的月亮，吹熄了灯，把小本子塞进枕头底下，压好了，这才睡下。这姑娘姓周，单名一个禾字。石坳村的人，都管她叫阿禾。

男弟子的大通铺上，鼾声一片。小满睡在最靠门的那张铺上，门缝里的风一夜往里灌。靠窗最好的那张铺，是马小宝的。他的家丁不许在山上过夜，傍晚便下山去了，可天黑以后，另有两个上一届的老弟子，嘴里带着酒气，蹲在他铺边上压着嗓子说话。小满只听清了几句：「……新来的一百多个，一人一块……」「……头一个月，三成归你……」「……那个杂灵根——」马小宝的声音：「他那块，我亲自收。」

小满把胸口的木牌掏出来，握在手心里。这一整天，它只烫了一回，就两个字，「左边」。今天是重阳，他娘在家里大约也插了茱萸，插完了数一数，少一个人。他对着木牌，小声说道：「现在打不过。他有荐书，有人，有他家的钱。我什么都没有。」停了一停，又道：「可是——账，我都记着呢。」

握在手心里的木牌，轻轻地，暖了一下。

窗外，外门的告示栏上，贴着一张新的告示，墨迹还没干：

**外门公中：新入门弟子，领了灵石，每人先交一块。明日一早，饭堂门口。**

落款三个字：马师兄。写这三个字的人，进山门还不到半天。
story.en:
Meanwhile, elsewhere. The girls' long bunk of the outer court was in another courtyard. That night, on the bunk nearest the wall, a lamp the size of a bean was still burning. Under it lay a girl with two little braids and a red nose, a freshly sharpened stick of charcoal in hand, writing stroke by stroke in a palm-sized notebook. What she wrote was:

The ninth of the ninth. Double Ninth.

The steps. Three hundred. Charged up; didn't sit. Two blisters on my feet — noted: left one, right one.

He was at the back, walking, not running. Three steps a breath, like his dad. Ma Xiaobao's chair blocked him; he crawled through underneath.

The Luo Shu. When I'd finished he was still staring. Then he got it right, half a stick of incense slower than me. The old steward asked him why; he said he reckoned it. Noted: he had a rhyme and still reckoned. I had no rhyme, only reckoning.

The forest. That thing had nine heads. I walked over with my eyes shut and touched the bark; I didn't look at it. He looked, and threw a stone. That roll to the right — I didn't understand it; like someone told him something. Noted: ask. Don't ask. Note it for now.

Someone of the Mas threw a pebble into the forest. I saw. The old sweeper saw too. Noted.

The stone. Me, three colours; they said above the middle. Him, five; they laughed. I didn't. Ma Xiaobao laughed three times — noted: three.

The places were full; he held up his tag and said one sentence, and the hall stopped laughing. Noted: he dares.

He didn't recognise me.

Mum said: go. Mum said: don't go the same road as him. Go alone and die, fine; go together and die, that's two, bad bargain. Mum said it and then cried. Dad took me the back way; we set out a day before them and slept under the temple veranda.

Noted: Mum owes me one not-crying.

Five taels. Little brother.

Thirty grains of seed rice, sewn into my jacket.

Dad carried me a stretch. Past the old locust, Dad said: "Past this tree, it's not our village any more." He set me down to walk on my own. I looked back once. That tree — eleven years I stood under it, and only today did I learn how small it looks from outside.

Noted: Shen Xiaoman owes me three and a half eggs. Interest, separate.

Writing this far, the lamp wick sputtered with a *pop*. The girl looked up at the moon outside the window, blew out the lamp, pushed the notebook under her pillow, pressed it flat, and only then lay down. The girl was surnamed Zhou, given name He — one character. The people of Shi'ao Village all called her Ahe.

On the boys' long bunk, snoring everywhere. Xiaoman slept in the bed nearest the door, the draught through the crack blowing in all night. The best bed, by the window, was Ma Xiaobao's. His servants weren't allowed to stay the night on the mountain and had gone down at dusk; but after dark two old disciples from the last intake, breath smelling of wine, squatted by his bed talking low. Xiaoman caught only a few words: "…the hundred-odd new ones, one each…" "…first month, thirty in the hundred is yours…" "…that mixed root —" Ma Xiaobao's voice: "His, I'll collect myself."

Xiaoman took the token from his chest and held it in his palm. All day it had burned once, two words: "Left." Today was Double Ninth; at home his mother would have put up dogwood, and counted when she'd done, and been one short. He said softly to the token: "Can't beat them now. He's got a letter, got people, got his family's money. I've got nothing." He stopped a moment, and said again: "But — I'm keeping the books on all of it."

The token in his palm, gently, warmed once.

Outside the window, on the outer court's notice board, a new notice had been posted, the ink not yet dry:

**Outer court common fund: new disciples, once you draw your spirit stones, pay one each first. Tomorrow morning, at the refectory door.**

Signed with three characters: Senior Brother Ma. The one who wrote them had been inside the gate less than half a day.

exits.means: rests, ends the day, or asks what comes next
